intro: Every business you walk past, from a food truck near the train to the company that sends your phone bill, is making the same kinds of decisions. How much should we make? What should we charge? Should we hire one more worker, buy a second machine, or close for the winter? And every business faces a market that is either crowded with rivals or nearly empty of them. This unit follows businesses from the inside out.

First you will open the books of a single firm. You will sort costs into fixed and variable, find average and marginal cost from a small table, see why adding workers to a fixed kitchen eventually adds less, and use the rule that marginal revenue should equal marginal cost. You will compare accounting profit with economic profit, find a break-even point, and weigh the trade-offs of sole proprietorships, partnerships, corporations and LLCs.

Then you will step back and look at whole markets. You will learn to size up any market with three questions: how many sellers, how hard it is to get in, and whether buyers can walk away. That sorts markets into perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and monopoly. By the end you will be able to explain why twenty pizza shops earn modest profits while one phone company in a small town does not, and what antitrust law and unions do about market power.
bigQuestion: How do firms decide how much to make and what to charge, and how does the number of competitors they face change those decisions?

timeline.t: Adam Smith describes the division of labor in a pin workshop in The Wealth of Nations
Antoine Augustin Cournot publishes a mathematical model of competition between two sellers
The Chicago Board of Trade is founded, later a center for trading grain prices
John D. Rockefeller and partners found Standard Oil in Ohio
Congress passes the Sherman Antitrust Act
The Pullman Strike begins in Chicago and spreads across the nation's railroads
The Supreme Court orders Standard Oil broken into 34 companies
Congress passes the Clayton Act and creates the Federal Trade Commission
Edward Chamberlin and Joan Robinson publish theories of competition between monopoly and perfect competition
The National Labor Relations Act gives most private-sector workers the right to organize
The Bell telephone system is broken up after a federal antitrust case

words.d: a cost that stays the same no matter how much the business produces, such as rent
a cost that rises and falls with the amount produced, such as ingredients
the extra cost of producing one more unit
the extra revenue from selling one more unit
total revenue minus both explicit costs and implicit costs such as the owner's opportunity cost
adding more of one input to a fixed input eventually adds less and less output
falling average cost per unit as a firm grows larger
owners can lose only what they invested, not their personal property
a firm's ability to raise its price above the competitive level without losing all its customers
anything that makes it hard for a new firm to start selling in a market
a market dominated by a few large firms, usually with high barriers to entry
a market with a single seller of a product with no close substitutes

test.q: A food truck sells 2,000 tacos at $3 each and has total costs of $4,500. What is its profit?
Which is a fixed cost for a hair salon?
choices: The monthly lease on the shop
Hourly pay for extra stylists on busy days
test.why: The lease is owed each month no matter how many haircuts the salon gives. The others rise with the number of customers.

test.q: Total cost is $200 at 10 units and $224 at 11 units. What is the marginal cost of the 11th unit?
test.why: Marginal cost is the change in total cost: $224 − $200 = $24.

test.q: An owner's shop has accounting profit of $50,000. She gave up a $40,000 job to run it. What is her economic profit?
test.why: Economic profit subtracts the implicit cost: $50,000 − $40,000 = $10,000.

test.q: A bakery adds a fourth baker to its one oven, and output rises by less than it did with the third baker. This shows
test.why: Adding workers to a fixed input, the oven, eventually adds less output per worker.

test.q: A firm's next unit has a marginal revenue of $12 and a marginal cost of $15. What should the firm do?
choices: Not make it, because it would lower profit by $3
test.why: When marginal cost is above marginal revenue, the extra unit subtracts $15 − $12 = $3 from profit.

test.q: Fixed costs are $3,000 a month, the price is $10 and variable cost is $4 a unit. What is the break-even quantity?
Which form of business protects its owners with limited liability and lets it raise money by selling stock to the public?
test.why: A corporation is a separate legal person, so shareholders risk only what they invest, and it can sell shares to many investors.

test.q: A wheat farmer is called a price taker because
choices: she can charge any price she likes
she is too small to affect the market price of an identical product
she takes the highest price offered
test.why: In perfect competition, each seller's output is a tiny share of an identical product, so she must accept the market price.

test.q: Nail salons in a city are many, easy to open, and each a little different. This market is
test.why: Many sellers, easy entry and differentiated products define monopolistic competition.

test.q: Three companies make nearly all of a country's airplanes, and each watches the others before changing prices. This market is
test.why: A few dominant firms whose choices depend on each other define an oligopoly.

test.q: Compared with a competitive market with the same costs, a monopoly tends to
choices: charge the same and sell the same
test.why: The monopoly stops where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, producing less than competition would and charging a higher price.

test.q: Which is the best reason a city's water system is a natural monopoly?
choices: Duplicate pipe networks would raise the average cost per home
test.why: With huge fixed costs, one network serving everyone has a lower average cost than two networks splitting the customers.

test.q: Which is illegal under Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act?
choices: Having 60% of a market because of a better product
Rival firms agreeing to fix prices
test.why: Section 1 bans agreements in restraint of trade, such as price fixing among competitors.

test.q: A union negotiates a contract for all the nurses at a hospital at once. This process is called
test.why: Collective bargaining is negotiation between a union and an employer on behalf of all the members.

write.prompt: A food truck owner earns $4,000 a month in accounting profit and gave up a $3,500 job. A second truck would add $2,000 a month in fixed costs and serve a busy stadium lot where two other trucks already park. Should she buy it? Use fixed and marginal costs, economic profit and the market structure she would face, with numbers.
tips: Separate fixed costs from variable costs, and leave out sunk costs.
Compute economic profit by subtracting her opportunity cost.
Find how many extra sales the second truck needs to break even.
Name the market structure at the stadium and say what entry by rivals will do to profits.
Name the biggest risk and the trade-off she is making.
